steps.body: With a shared denominator, ordering three fractions is ordering three counts — the pieces are identical, so only the tally differs.
steps.narration: With a shared denominator, ordering three fractions is ordering three counts — the pieces are identical, so only the tally differs.

widget.prompt: Build the largest unit fraction among 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6.
widget.successFeedback: 1/3 — the fewest pieces means the biggest piece.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded bar is shorter than the target half. Shade more — raise the numerator, or use fewer parts.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded bar is longer than half. Shade less — lower the numerator, or split into more parts.

commonFractions.feedback: 1/6 splits the whole into the most pieces, so its piece is the smallest of the three.
1/4 sits between; thirds are cut fewer times and stay larger.

predict.prompt: Order 1/3, 1/4, 1/6 from least to greatest. Which is least?
predict.reveal: Six pieces in one whole are the smallest pieces here, so 1/6 is the least.

cml.actionGoal: Cut, count, and compare equal pieces to see what g3f order three really names.
invariants: A fraction names equal shares of ONE whole: the denominator says how many equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts them, which is what makes g3f order three comparable at all.
misconceptions: Calling unequal pieces fractions, reading the denominator as a count, or comparing fractions that came from different-sized wholes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the whole changed size, which of these comparisons would stop being trustworthy?

widget.prompt: Order 3/6, 5/6, and 4/6 from least to greatest. Which one is in the MIDDLE?

options.feedback: Correct — with identical sixth-size pieces, ordering the counts orders the fractions, and 4 sits between 3 and 5.
3/6 holds the FEWEST pieces, so it is the least, not the middle.
5/6 holds the MOST pieces, so it is the greatest, not the middle.

1/3 has the fewest pieces so each is largest — it comes LAST, not second.
